source.passage:
Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

adapted.passage:
Kellerman's boatyard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. His boat, the Marisol, sat on blocks in the shed. My grandfather built her, and Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life.

By Monday, every family on the lake had an idea for what to do with her. By Friday, she had a new owner. The sailing club had asked in June to use her for teaching beginners. "A gift pays no debt," he told them, and no beginner ever stepped aboard. Petrus rowed over to offer his small boat and motor in a trade. Teodor could still handle the Marisol by himself, and he said a trade brings no money through the gate. Back in June, he had pushed a knife into her planks near the keel. The blade would not sink in even a quarter inch, and there was no rot anywhere. In the end, the marina at Two Harbours sent a check, and he signed it over to the bank.

The bank had held a loan on the yard since the bad winter, and the amount owed had grown larger than a whole season of repairs could earn. Every other plan that week hit the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would never open again. "The yard will outlast any boat in it," he said. "I will not close these doors to keep one hull in the family."

The sale drew half the people on the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried out chairs for strangers. I had argued against the sale all week. When a neighbor told me my uncle had done the brave thing, I walked away without a word. I was furious with him all evening. I kept bringing it up at dinner long after he had stopped answering, and my jaw stayed tight the whole night. Even then, I knew it was not fair to blame him. That check was the yard's only chance.

source.passage: The tolls charged on eighteenth-century English canals were fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act, which set both a ceiling and a floor: a company could charge no more than the published schedule, and could not carry one merchant's coal for less than it charged another for the same cargo. Historians have lately made the floor the traders' device, a guarantee that no rival would be given a better rate. The petitions tell it the other way. Those asking for the floors came from the companies, whose shareholders wanted an end to rate-cutting between rival canals. The traders' petitions do not mention the floor at all; they ask that the maxima be cut, and they complain of each revision of the act since, for a rate stood where the act had put it until Parliament moved it, and Parliament had moved it upward every time. What the traders feared was ______ tolls.

adapted.passage: In the 1700s, Parliament set the tolls on each English canal in a law. The law set a top price and a bottom price. A company could not charge more than the published list. Nor could it charge one trader less than another for the same load. Some historians say the bottom price was the traders' idea, so no rival could get a better deal. But the canal companies asked for the bottom price. The traders' petitions never mention it. They asked for lower top prices, and complained about every change to the law. A toll stayed where the law put it until Parliament changed it, and Parliament had raised it every time. What the traders feared was ______ tolls.

source.passage: The 'resource curse'—the observation that nations rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than resource-poor peers—is frequently taken to show that natural wealth is economically corrosive in itself. Some economists argue the correlation is misattributed. In their account, resource windfalls do not degrade otherwise sound institutions; rather, they tend to arrive in countries whose institutions were already weak, and merely make the consequences of that weakness more visible and better funded. Where accountable institutions predate a discovery, they find, windfalls are managed without any subsequent decline in growth. The curse, on this view, is not a property of the resource but a preexisting condition the resource exposes. What looks like wealth causing dysfunction is dysfunction determining how wealth is used.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument advanced in the text?
choices: In several countries, growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery.
A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.
Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies than countries dependent on a single export such as oil or minerals.
Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions of countries that were well governed before a discovery.
source.key: A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.

adapted.passage: Countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than countries without them. This pattern, called the "resource curse," is often taken to show that natural wealth harms an economy by itself. Some economists disagree. In their view, sudden resource wealth does not damage a country's institutions, such as its courts and government, if they were already sound. Instead, the wealth tends to arrive in countries whose institutions were already weak. It just makes that weakness easier to see and better funded. Where accountable institutions existed before a discovery, these economists found, growth did not drop afterward. On this view, the curse is not caused by the resource. It is an older problem that the resource exposes.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument in the passage?
choices: In several countries, growth fell sharply in the years right after a big mineral find.
A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.
Countries with strong institutions tend to make and sell more kinds of goods than countries that rely on one export.
Sudden resource wealth has been shown to weaken institutions in countries that were well run before a find.
adapted.key: A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.
